title: Predicting player churn in an MMORPG (WoW)
text:
In this blog post we will see how we can predict player churn in World of Warcraft (WoW), a subscription-based MMORPG that was released in 2004. More precisely, we are interested in predicting a player’s behavior in a given month, and decide whether there is a risk that they will stop playing the next month. To do so, we want to train a machine learning model that, given features based on each player and on the overall playerbase, will be able to predict whether player X will stop playing in a given month.
Through the post we will build a full machine learning pipeline: we use
polars for dataframe operations; skrub is used for data exploration, feature engineering and constructing the overall execution plan; scikit-learn is imported for the actual ML model; hyperparameter optimization is done using Optuna through skrub’s Data Ops.
To keep the focus of this post on the process rather than the code, most of the lower-level functions will be hidden in collapsible blocks. This includes much of the pre-processing and feature engineering, although important sections will be highlighted as needed. Additionally, some detail on the implementation will be omitted from this writeup; for detailed comments and rationale on the code refer to the repository.

title: Predicting player churn in an MMORPG (WoW)
text:
1 Modeling player churn
Modeling user churn is a common application of machine learning models, though the definition of churn is typically business’ specific. In general, by “user churn” one refers to “a user that does not come back to the service”. In the context of WoW, user churn would refer to those users that do not come back to the game and suspend their monthly subscription. As we do not have access to the actual subscription data, we assume that each player suspends their subscription as soon as they stop playing for a month.
For this post, we aggregate player behaviors at a monthly basis, and add a has_played flag that tells us if a player has played at during each month.






Important



Our objective
Given a month (e.g., June), we want to use all the data up to the last day of the previous month (all months until May included) to predict whether a user will churn in July (i.e., their has_played flag will be False in July).


The idea is that, by knowing that user X will churn in July, we should be able to use the month of June to apply some incentive to the user so they won’t churn.
One caveat with this modeling strategy is that we are working with historical data, so we cannot actually apply said incentive and observe whether it has an impact like in a typical A/B test.

1.1 Building the churn dataset
We begin by adding two columns to the historical dataset: in the first we store each timestamp, truncated to have a monthly resolution; in the second we track the first month for each character. Additionally, we add a constant has_played column that acts as our “player was seen” flag.
Since we are interested in monthly snapshots, the dataset is then reduced to select only the unique (character, month) pairs.






NoneData preparation (click to expand)






def make_data(df):
    """
    Add a timestamp column with monthly resolution, the first month for each
    character, and a constant column that acts as flag. 
    """

    data = (
        df.with_columns(
            pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate("1mo").alias("month"),
            first_month=pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate("1mo").min().over("char"),
        )
        .unique(subset=["char", "month"])
        .with_columns(pl.lit(True).alias("has_played"))
    )
    return data
data = make_data(df)




Since we want to predict the behavior a player will have over a single month, our target variable will be grouped by “user-month” (e.g., 153_2026-12). However, not all players will play at least once every month, so by relying exclusively on the historical data we would be missing samples; to get around this problem we generate a char_month dataset that contains all unique combinations of users and months by executing the cross-product between the unique users and the range of months.






NoneCross product (click to expand)





The cross product between two sets (in this case, months and unique users) builds a new set where each element in the first set is paired with all elements in the second set.

def make_user_month(df):
    """
    Create a DataFrame with all unique combinations of users and months.
    
    The month range is extracted from the dataset.  
    """

    months = pl.datetime_range(
        start=df.select(pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate("1mo").min()).collect().item(),
        end=df.select(pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate("1mo").max()).collect().item(),
        interval="1mo",
        closed="both",
        eager=True,
    )

    char_month = (
        df
        .select("char")
        .unique()
        .join(months.to_frame(name="month").lazy(), how="cross")
    )
    return char_month

user_month = make_user_month(df)
user_month.collect()

Now that we have all the combinations (character, month), we can join back the prepared data to mark all the months in which each character was found online, and marking all others with has_played=False.
Additionally, the resulting rows are filtered to remove all pairs (char, month) whose month precedes the character’s first month. We should not have a row about a character’s playtime in January if they started playing in August!






NoneAdd churn as a “has played” column (click to expand)






def add_churn(user_month, data):
    """
    Merge the user-month DataFrame with the actual play data.
    The resulting DataFrame will have a "has_played" column indicating
    whether the user played in that month. Any missing values in "has_played" are
    filled with False: missing values mean that the player did not play in that
    particular month.
    """

    df_with_user_month = (
        user_month.join(
            data,
            on=["char", "month"],
            how="left",
        )
        .with_columns(pl.col("has_played").fill_null(False))
        # Fill missing values in the first_month column with each character's
        # first month
        .with_columns(first_month=pl.col("first_month").min().over("char"))
        # Remove (char, month) rows where the month precedes the character's
        # first month
        .filter(pl.col("first_month") <= pl.col("month"))
        .select(
            "char",
            "month",
            "has_played",
            "first_month",
        )
    )
    return df_with_user_month

Finally, we can put everything together in a single function that takes the historical data as input and returns a dataset with the churn indication as output:

def build_churn_dataset(historical_data):
    # Load the dataset
    data = make_data(historical_data)
    # Add the combinations of user months
    user_month = make_user_month(historical_data)
    churn_data = add_churn(user_month, data)
    return churn_data

title: Predicting player churn in an MMORPG (WoW)
text:
2 Setting up the ML pipeline
Before starting with feature engineering and actually training the model, it’s worth spending some time understanding the scenario we are in.
The main factor that complicates this scenario is the fact that we are dealing with sequential data points, which are therefore not independent of each other: the position of a player at a time T is strongly correlated with their position at time T+1.

2.1 Building a custom splitter
For this reason, we need to use a splitter that returns sequential splits. A common example of this is scikit-learn’s TimeSeriesSplit. TimeSeriesSplit works by splitting the entire dataset in a given number of splits; during cross-validation, at step K the splitter returns the first k splits as the train split, and the k+1 split as the validation split.





Source
A downside of TimeSeriesSplit is that the splitter assumes uniformly distributed samples, so that each singular split has the same size as the others. This is a problem for our scenario: our samples are (character, month) pairs, and the number of characters in each month is never constant and indeed increases over time:





For this reason, we need to define a custom splitter that is aware of the constraints we are working with. Given that we are working month-by-month, each split should contain all the characters that played in a specific month, and should be able to do so regardless of the fact that the number of characters changes.
This is what we implement here:

from datetime import datetime

# We define the boundaries of the experiment manually
MIN_DATE = datetime.strptime("2008-01-01", "%Y-%m-%d")
MAX_DATE = datetime.strptime("2008-12-30", "%Y-%m-%d")

class Splitter:
    """
    This splitter iterates over the months. It selects all the months up to the 
    split point, which is our cutoff point: it's when we want to perform some 
    operation on users that are marked as "churn risk", i.e., have been predicted
    to churn by the model. 
    """
    def split(self, user_month, has_played=None):
        """
        user_month is our "X", while has_played is the target variable we want 
        to predict
        """
        # has_played is not needed by this splitter, we are only splitting by month
        del has_played
        time_range = pl.date_range(MIN_DATE, MAX_DATE, "1mo", eager=True)
        for split_point in time_range:
            # The test month is the month *after* the split point
            test_month = pl.Series([split_point]).dt.offset_by("1mo").first()
            # Train indices are up to split_point
            # We want a one-month gap
            train_idx = (
                user_month.with_row_index("idx")
                .filter(pl.col("month") <= split_point)["idx"]
                .to_list()
            )
            # Test indices are for the month after split_point
            test_idx = (
                user_month.with_row_index("idx")
                .filter(pl.col("month") == test_month)["idx"]
                .to_list()
            )
            if train_idx and test_idx:
                print(f"Working on month {split_point}")
                yield train_idx, test_idx

    def get_n_splits(self, X, y):
        return sum(1 for _ in self.split(X, y))

Like all other scikit-learn splitters, our splitter is a generator that, given X and y (user_month and has_played in our case), returns the indices of the samples that should be used in each split.

text:
3 Building the pipeline

3.1 Generating the features






NoneFull feature engineering function (click to expand)






# %%
# This function is needed to make sure that we are only ever using historical data
# up to the given month - 1 month. This is to avoid any leakage in the data.
def add_features(X, historical_data, session_gap=30, use_location=True, add_gini=False):
    features_by_month = []

    # Create a session encoder with a 30 minute timeout
    # This encoder is used as a stateless transformer so it is refitted for every
    # month
    session_encoder = SessionEncoder(
        split_by="char", timestamp_col="timestamp", session_gap=session_gap
    )
    historical_data = historical_data.with_columns(
        month=pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate("1mo")
    )
    last_month = X["month"].max()

    # Grouping by character and zone so that I can get the time spent in each zone
    # Even if users leave the zone, this lets me find how much time a user spends in
    # a given zone
    session_encoder_zone = SessionEncoder(
        split_by=["char", "zone"], timestamp_col="timestamp", session_gap=session_gap
    )
    # Adding fixed features: these features are fixed by character so they don't
    # change over time.
    # historical_data is selected up until the last month because if I select only
    # a single month then any character that did not play in that month will be
    # missing those features
    X = X.join(
        historical_data.filter(pl.col("month") <= last_month)
        .select("char", "race", "charclass")
        .unique("char"),
        on="char",
        how="left",
        maintain_order="left",
    ).with_row_index()  # adding row index so that I can reorder at the end after
    # concatenating
    # kinda defeats the point of using data ops but I think it simplifies the code

    # This is used to add the historical data up to the given month
    # Sorting months is not needed, but forces a consistent order (better for debugging)
    for month in X["month"].unique().sort():
        this_month_X = filter_df_by_month(X, month)

        # Selecting only the entries in the historical data whose month + 2 is equal
        # to the month I am trying to predict on.
        # This means that if the "target month" is April, then the historical data
        # should be filtered to keep only the rows where the current month + 2
        # is equal to April, that is, the month is February. This is equivalent
        # to saying "I want the rows for the current month - 2 months", but it's
        # easier to implement
        kept_historical_data = historical_data.with_columns(
            pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("2mo")
        ).filter(pl.col("month") == month)

        # Session features: a session starts from a heartbeat, then it ends when
        # no more heartbeats are detected for session_gap minutes
        historical_data_with_sessions = session_encoder.fit_transform(
            kept_historical_data
        )
        historical_data_with_sessions = get_session_duration(
            historical_data_with_sessions
        )

        # General features: add session based and playerbase features
        df_with_features = add_general_features(
            this_month_X, historical_data_with_sessions
        )

        # Location features can be useful but take much longer to generate
        if use_location:
            # Zone-session features: a session lasts from the first time a character
            # enters a zone to the moment it leaves it
            # This is useful to get zone-specific features
            historical_data_zone_sessions = session_encoder_zone.fit_transform(
                kept_historical_data
            )
            historical_data_zone_sessions = get_session_duration(
                historical_data_zone_sessions
            )
            df_with_features = add_location_features(
                df_with_features,
                historical_data_zone_sessions,
                add_gini=add_gini,
            )

        features_by_month.append(df_with_features)
        assert len(df_with_features) == len(this_month_X)

    X_res = pl.concat(features_by_month, how="vertical")
    X_res = X_res.sort("index").drop("index")

    return X_res






3.2 Putting everything together in a Data Op






TipLoading and downsampling the file (click to expand)





The dataset is very large, so we downsample it to reduce the execution time. Note that we need to be deliberate with how we sample the data: rather than choosing a random subset of the values in the dataset, we need to be careful to select a subset of characters and keep all the rows for those characters. This ensures that we have reliable information about all the characters.

def sample_by_char(df, fraction=0.1):
    """
    Sample a fraction of chars and return all their data.
    """
    data = df.filter(
        pl.col("char").is_in(
            df.select(pl.col("char").unique())
            .sample(fraction=fraction, seed=42)["char"]
            .implode()
        )
    )
    return data


def load(file, fraction=0.1):
    if fraction == 1:
        print("Returning all users")
        return pl.scan_parquet(file)

    print(f"Sampling {fraction * 100}% of the users")
    df = pl.scan_parquet(file)
    df = sample_by_char(df.collect(), fraction=fraction)
    return df.lazy()










TipFull Data Op construction script




# %%a
import skrub

def make_data_op():
    historical_data_file = skrub.var("historical_data_file")
    historical_data = historical_data_file.skb.apply_func(load)
    # In the guild column, null values are denoted by -1. This step replaces -1
    # with None. 
    historical_data = historical_data.with_columns(
        pl.when(pl.col("guild") == -1)
        .then(None)
        .otherwise(pl.col("guild"))
        .alias("guild")
    )

    user_month_has_played = historical_data.skb.apply_func(build_churn_dataset)
    X = user_month_has_played["char", "month"].skb.mark_as_X(cv=Splitter())
    y = user_month_has_played["has_played"].skb.mark_as_y()

    # Hyperparameters
    session_gap = skrub.choose_from([60], name="session_gap")
    use_location = skrub.choose_bool(name="location_features")
    add_gini = skrub.choose_bool(name="add_gini")

    all_features = X.skb.apply_func(
        add_features,
        historical_data.collect(),
        session_gap=session_gap,
        use_location=use_location,
        add_gini=add_gini
    )
    encoded = all_features.skb.apply(skrub.TableVectorizer())
    # data_op = encoded.skb.apply(SimpleImputer()).skb.apply(LogisticRegression(), y=y)
    data_op = encoded.skb.apply(
        HGB(learning_rate=skrub.choose_float(0.01, 1.0, log=True)), y=y
    )
    # data_op = encoded.skb.apply(DummyClassifier(), y=y)
    return data_op

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
text:
The example in one slide

Dataset: WoWAH — ~11M timestamped “heartbeats” (one snapshot every ~10 min, 2006–2009, 91k avatars)
Task: predict whether a player churns (no activity) in month M+1
Unit of analysis: the (character, month) pair, built as a cross-product grid
Features: sessionization (SessionEncoder), monthly aggregates, zone-rarity / Gini location features, lag & diff features
Model: HistGradientBoostingClassifier + TableVectorizer, month-by-month temporal CV
Glue: everything assembled as a single skrub Data Op


The pipeline lives in main.py (with draft.qmd as the write-up version). It loads raw logs from a parquet file, builds churn labels with add_churn.py, engineers features in adding_features.py / location_features.py, and assembles the whole thing into a skrub DataOp via make_data_op(). Each of the following slides is a pain point a data scientist hits in this kind of project, and how the skrub DataOps design (per the user guide in skrub/_docs/) addresses it.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
section: Pain point 1 — Leakage in temporal feature engineering
text:
Pain point 1 — Leakage in temporal feature engineering

Features must only use data available at scoring time: history is filtered with a 2-month offset before the target month
Session detection and aggregations are stateful w.r.t. time: doing them once on the full table leaks the future
sklearn Pipeline cannot do this: X/y must exist before the pipeline starts, and wrangling lives outside
skrub docs warn explicitly: aggregation can introduce data leakage → wrap it in the DataOps plan
In the example: X and y are cut inside the plan (mark_as_X / mark_as_y), so each CV fold re-runs the feature code on training data only


This is the central difficulty of the example (main.py:90-186). If the target month is April, features may only be built from February data and earlier (main.py:136-143). The skrub sessionization doc (modules/multi_column_operations/sessionization.rst) carries a warning box saying aggregation leaks unless it is re-fit per fold — either wrapped in an sklearn transformer or done “with the skrub Data Ops framework”. DataOps bind the whole wrangling DAG to the prediction, so skb.cross_validate() re-executes the leakage-safe steps inside every fold automatically, instead of the user hand-rolling fold-by-fold feature construction.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
section: Pain point 2 — Cross-validation that respects irregular time
text:
Pain point 2 — Cross-validation that respects irregular time

Off-the-shelf TimeSeriesSplit assumes folds of equal size
Here the number of (char, month) rows grows every month — folds are unbalanced by nature
So the repo writes a custom splitter: expanding window over months, test = the following month only (main.py:46-74)
With DataOps: one line plugs it in — skb.mark_as_X(cv=Splitter())
The same splitter is then honored by cross_validate, train_test_split, randomized search, and scoring — no per-fold orchestration code


The custom Splitter (main.py:46) iterates month by month, yields train indices up to the split point and test indices for the next month. In a vanilla setup, the user would have to drive CV manually (loop over folds, build features per fold, fit, score). In the DataOps plan, mark_as_X(cv=Splitter()) (main.py:219) makes the splitter part of the estimator-like object, so skb.cross_validate() (main.py:259) and the Optuna search reuse it consistently. The docs (tuning_validating_data_ops.rst) also show how extra splitter arguments (e.g. groups) can be passed through mark_as_X.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
section: Pain point 3 — Tuning wrangling choices, not just model knobs
text:
Pain point 3 — Tuning wrangling choices, not just model knobs

Real choices live in the feature code: session_gap (15/30/60 min), include location features?, add Gini?, which lags?
These are not model hyperparameters — they are data pipeline decisions with big performance and runtime impact
DataOps: drop choices inline where the value is used — choose_from, choose_bool, choose_float(log=True)
One call turns the whole DAG into a search: skb.make_randomized_search(backend="optuna", ...) (main.py:267-280)
The repo shows the payoff: a persistent Optuna study (wowah_churn_study.db), results inspectable across runs


In make_data_op() (main.py:222-228), session_gap, use_location, add_gini and lags are declared with choose_from / choose_bool, and the model’s learning_rate with choose_float(0.1, 0.5, log=True). The hyperparameter tuning doc (validation/hyperparameter_tuning.rst) explains the principle: replace values with choice objects, and the same plan serves previews, defaults (describe_defaults), grid/randomized search, and Optuna. Crucially, choices placed inside wrangling functions get tuned too — impossible with a vanilla sklearn grid search over the final estimator.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
section: Pain point 4 — One pipeline object, many inputs, deployable
text:
Pain point 4 — One pipeline object, many inputs, deployable

Multi-input pipelines (raw log file path, churn table, config) are usually scattered across scripts with brittle glue
The example treats even the file path as an input: skrub.var("historical_data_file")
apply_func inserts arbitrary Python (loading, sampling, churn-label construction) as graph nodes
The final DataOp behaves like one sklearn estimator: .fit(), save, load, skb.eval(env), skb.cross_validate(env)
Production: replay the exact trained DAG on a new month — no re-implementation drift


make_data_op() (main.py:206) starts from a path variable, applies load (which subsamples by user), fixes the guild == -1 sentinel, builds churn labels, marks X/y, adds features, vectorizes, and fits HGB — one object. cross_validate() and evaluate() just pass different environments ({"historical_data_file": ...}) to the same plan (main.py:259-287). The docs’ what_are_data_ops.rst frames this as: a DataOp is a complete pipeline from data loading to prediction that can be fitted, tuned, cross-validated and saved like a scikit-learn estimator; data_ops_vs_alternatives.rst contrasts this with Pipeline, which is a linear sequence on a single table with a fixed row count.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
section: Pain point 5 — Debugging a complex DAG
text:
Pain point 5 — Debugging a complex DAG

With cross-products, two SessionEncoders, joins, lags… a join bug surfaces far from its cause
Eager previews: pass a value to var() and every node shows its result immediately — errors surface at the offending step
skb.full_report() emits an HTML report: every node’s name, description, predecessors, fitted estimator, and data preview
On failure, the report shows the offending node and the traceback
describe_steps, describe_param_grid, describe_defaults document the plan as it grows


The example’s pipeline has deep, branchy nodes (churn cross-product grid, session and zone-session encoders, rarity/Gini features, lag/diff expansion). The docs (basics/using_previews.rst, ml_pipeline/evaluating_debugging_data_ops.rst) describe exactly this workflow: previews catch errors early (e.g. a wrong column name in a Polars expression fails right away), and full_report() produces a browsable HTML execution report (stored under skrub_data/execution_reports by default). This replaces the usual print/pytest-debug loop on a multi-stage dataframe pipeline.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
section: Pain point 6 — Big data: subsampling and caching
text:
Pain point 6 — Big data: subsampling and caching

11M rows → interactive development must be fast, but sampling must preserve players’ full trajectories (sample_by_user, not random rows)
Feature building (build_feature_table) is very expensive — naive re-runs during search would explode cost
DataOps: skb.subsample() for development is automatically off for real eval / cross_validate runs
Caching (skrub.set_config(cache=True)) persists expensive node results on disk across trials — changing only learning_rate doesn’t recompute features
In-memory reuse is free: the feature_table node is computed once per parameter set and shared (main.py:229-239)


load() (main.py:196-202) samples whole characters to keep trajectories intact — exactly the kind of domain-specific subsampling the docs’ subsampling page (ml_pipeline/subsampling_data.rst) anticipates, with the caveat that subsampling is “local” to the variable it is applied to. The caching doc (ml_pipeline/caching.rst) is the counterpart for cost: results of skb.apply / skb.apply_func nodes are keyed and persisted, so hyperparameter trials that share early steps (all feature construction) skip recomputation; no_cache=True and cache pruning (target_cache_size) give control. Caveat from the docs: cache invalidation of changed helper code is best-effort — delete the cache when actively editing.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
section: Pain point 7 — Stay in your dataframe API inside the plan
text:
Pain point 7 — Stay in your dataframe API inside the plan

Frameworks usually force you to leave Polars once you enter “pipeline land”
DataOps are transparent: Polars methods are called directly on DataOps (historical_data.with_columns(...), .collect(), indexing, joins)
Python control flow (for month in ...) can’t run eagerly on a DataOp → put it in @deferred / apply_func functions
Each such function appears as one graph node — good for reports and caching granularity
The example leans on this everywhere: build_churn_dataset, build_feature_table, add_features


basics/direct_access_methods.rst documents the “transparent DataOp” design: any non-.skb attribute/method goes to the underlying object, so the example writes idiomatic Polars throughout (main.py:211-216). basics/control_flow.rst explains the eager-vs-deferred rule: for over a DataOp raises, so loops live inside @skrub.deferred functions or are attached via skb.apply_func — in the example the whole per-month feature loop is deferred into build_feature_table (main.py:90). One hygiene rule from the docs: transformations must return new values, not mutate in place — Polars’ expression style fits this naturally.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
text:
The open tension (discussion)

main.py precomputes feature_table once on the full history, then joins it onto each fold’s X
Why: lag/diff features need each character’s complete monthly timeline — a single-month fold would leave every lag null (main.py:82-89 comment)
But the write-up admits: “kinda defeats the point of using data ops but I think it simplifies the code” (draft.qmd:419)
Strict per-fold feature building is leakage-proof but slow; the static table is fast but frozen per hyperparameter set
DataOps makes this trade-off explicit and inspectable: the DAG documents exactly what is recomputed per fold vs. cached/shared


This is the design decision the example is really about. Two strategies coexist: (1) build features inside the graph from X (draft.qmd’s add_features loop) — perfectly leakage-safe, recomputed per fold; (2) precompute a feature_table node from the full historical data (main.py:229-239) so lagged features see all months, then left-join each fold’s rows. Option (2) relies on the argument that features are keyed by (char, month ≤ cutoff) so no future data can leak into the fold’s rows — but the plan no longer enforces it mechanically; the guarantee lives in build_feature_table’s code. A natural follow-up: move the per-month filtering inside the plan and use skrub caching to recover speed, so leakage safety is structural rather than conventional.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
text:
Takeaways



Pain point
skrub DataOps answer




Temporal leakage
Wrangling lives inside the plan, re-run per fold


Irregular time CV
Custom splitter via mark_as_X(cv=...)


Tuning data choices
choose_* inline + Optuna-backed search


Many inputs, one artifact
var() + one estimator-like DataOp


Debugging
Previews + full_report() per node


Big data
subsample() + disk caching


API freedom
Transparent Polars access, @deferred for logic




Closing summary: the sessionization example is a good stress test because it combines every hard part of applied ML — temporal structure, custom validation, heavy feature engineering, big data, and tuning of pipeline-level decisions. The skrub DataOps docs position the framework precisely where sklearn Pipeline stops: DAG-shaped, multi-input, leakage-aware, tunable end-to-end, and inspectable. The remaining open question (per-fold vs. precomputed features) is itself made visible by the plan structure rather than hidden in scripts.
